What moved yields
India: hawkish minutes from the RBI's August meeting revived rate-hike expectations for later this year — Deputy Governor Poonam Gupta said there's "no scope for further policy easing," and Governor Malhotra flagged broader inflation risks from food, fuel and input prices. This pushed the benchmark 6.94% 2036 bond to its highest intraday level since June 18, ahead of a ₹340 billion bond auction. Partially offsetting: Brent crude fell ~5% this week on renewed Strait-of-Hormuz reopening talk, easing some inflation pressure. US: yields were little changed through the week as markets awaited Warsh's first Jackson Hole speech as Fed Chair — short-end yields (2Y) jumped after he reaffirmed his commitment to lowering inflation, while the 10Y stayed comparatively steady.
05

Executive Summary — Where Is Institutional Money Flowing?

Two lenses on the same question — where did money move this week, and across which markets (US, India, Global, Commodity)?

5.1 — Global: Macros, Commodities, US Stocks, US & Global ETFs

The big picture — Global
Money broadly de-risked out of both commodities and US equities this week, while the dollar weakened against most currencies including the rupee. The clearest signal is the sharp reversal in metals: Gold Miners ETF flipped from last week's best performer (+14.3%) to this week's worst (-3.1%), and the broader Global ETF breadth flipped from 35 advancers/12 decliners to 19/28 — a swing from strongly risk-on to risk-off in commodity-linked assets in a single week. US equities told a similar story: only 384 of 957 stocks (40%) were positive, the weakest US breadth reading tracked in this report so far, even as the broader US ETF universe (4,609 funds, mostly bonds/fixed-income) stayed more resilient — suggesting the outflow was concentrated in growth/commodity-sensitive equities rather than a blanket flight from all US assets.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's first Jackson Hole speech as chair (Thu-Fri) dominated the macro narrative — he reaffirmed a commitment to bringing down inflation that's "not meaningfully improved," which pushed short-end US Treasury yields up sharply (2Y +6bps) while the 10Y stayed comparatively steady (~4.68%). Markets are now pricing higher odds of a Fed move as soon as next month. Despite a hawkish Fed setting up dollar strength, the rupee and most other tracked currencies actually gained against the dollar this week — a disconnect worth watching, since it suggests EM currency demand or India-specific flows outweighed the usual dollar-supportive effect of hawkish Fed commentary, at least for now.

Read together: this looks like a rotation out of commodity/metals exposure and weaker US equities into cash or safer assets, ahead of/around a hawkish Fed signal — not a broad "risk-off everywhere" move, since bond-heavy ETFs and the rupee both held up.

5.2 — India: Macros, Indices, Sectors, Stocks

The big picture — India
Domestic institutional money kept flowing in at a record pace, even as foreign money and the index itself both softened. DII bought a record +₹19,309 Cr this week — the second straight week setting a new high for this report — while FII sold -₹2,059 Cr, a second consecutive negative week. Unlike the prior two weeks where DII buying fully offset FII selling in price terms, Nifty 50 fell again this week (-0.31%, a third straight down week, though each week's decline has been milder than the last: -0.83% → -0.47% → -0.31%). Breadth softened slightly (740 Adv/848 Dec vs last week's 759/808).

Domestic bond yields rose this week on hawkish RBI policy minutes reviving rate-hike expectations — India's 10Y G-Sec climbed to a near-2-month high (~6.87-6.91%), even as softer Brent crude (-5% this week) offered some offsetting relief on the inflation side. This is a notable divergence from equities: bond markets are pricing in tighter policy ahead, while DII buying in equities remains as aggressive as it's been all report.

At the stock level, breadth signals are mixed: DMA200 crossovers stayed roughly flat (54 above vs 50 below, net +4), but DMA50 crossovers turned more negative (99 above vs 119 below, net -20, worse than last week's -4) — early signs the stabilization seen two weeks ago may be fading at the shorter-term momentum level, even as the 52-week-high list kept growing (154→161 names), so it isn't a uniformly bearish picture.

Read together: India money flow this week was "DII in, FII out, bond yields up" — a pattern where domestic conviction remains strong even as the marginal foreign investor and the bond market both turned more cautious. Worth watching whether rising domestic yields eventually compete with equities for DII allocation if the RBI's hawkish tilt continues.

Net read — where did the money move this week?
Out of: commodity/metals exposure (sharp Global ETF reversal), weaker US equities (worst US breadth yet), and — mildly — FII positioning in India. Into: India via DII (record buying, second week running), and apparently into the rupee and most non-USD currencies despite a hawkish Fed. Rotating within: US markets, where equity weakness didn't extend to the broader (bond-heavy) ETF universe. The through-line is a hawkish-Fed-driven reassessment that hit commodities and richly-valued US equities hardest, while India's domestic buying pace and currency both showed resilience.

Global ETF Heatmap — Weekly Analysis

Executive Summary — Weekly Change

The big picture
A sharp reversal from last week — metals miners flipped from the best performers to among the worst, and breadth turned negative. Only 19 of 47 ETFs were positive (down from 35 last week). Taiwan (+3.45%) and Saudi Arabia (+2.48%) led; Gold Miners, last week's top performer at +14.29%, fell to dead last at -3.09% — one of the sharpest single-week reversals seen in this report. Middle East was the only region with a positive average (+1.44%), while Africa (-2.47%, single constituent) and Global (-1.83%, dragged down by gold/uranium miners) lagged.
